meta.title: The Art of Perfumery, and Methods of Obtaining the Odors of Plants
meta.author: G. W. Septimus Piesse

parts.title: The Art of Perfumery: An Introduction to the Underestimated Sense of Smell

sentences: The **sense of smell** is important, though often **undervalued**, and is crucial for **health and well-being**.
Ignoring this sense can lead to inhaling **impure air**, and perfume users are **more sensitive** to vitiated atmospheres.
Historically, perfumes were widely used and held **Scriptural authority**, with their patrons being considered **civilized and refined**.
Pathologically, perfumes are **prophylactic**, and citrine odors aid invalids.
There is a **lack of flower-farms in England** for perfume production, making the country reliant on foreign imports, and more local cultivation is needed.
**Economic potential** is lost by English horticulturists who do not extract scents from their flowers, similar to early Cornish miners discarding copper ore.
Content from "Gardeners' Chronicle" and "Annals of Pharmacy and Chemistry" has been used for this comprehensive book, with thanks extended to several individuals for their assistance.

parts.title: The Historical and Commercial Significance of Perfumes and Perfumery Processes

sentences: **Incense** is widely used in the **Romish Church**, especially at high-ranking funerals.
Historically, various cultures, like **Ancient Egyptians** and **Chinese**, used perfumed gums and scented beads.
The **book of Exodus** details instructions for making holy incense, inspiring the comparison of prayers to ascending incense.
The **Magi** presented frankincense to Jesus, and **Primitive Christians** adopted incense in their Liturgy.
Its use is **perpetual** in **Oriental churches**, with **Coptic and other Eastern Christians** following Latin Church rituals.
Perfumes were also used in church oils and waxes, creating fragrance around **martyrs' sepulchres**.
**Constantine the Great** and **St. Paulinus of Nola** noted these practices.
The **Frangipani perfume**, a powder, was invented by a **Roman noble**.
The **trade in perfume-drugs** boosted commerce in regions like the Red Sea.
**Southern Italy** became a center for perfumers.
**English perfumery** hasn't excelled due to secrecy, though **Professor Solly** advocated knowledge sharing.
Flowers in **warmer latitudes** are more fragrant.
The **South of Europe** is the main perfumery hub due to its ideal climate for plants like Cassia and violets.
**England excels** in lavender and peppermint oils.
Plant odors come from **roots, stem/wood, leaves, flowers, seeds, and bark**.
The **orange tree** provides multiple distinct odors.
Plant fragrance comes from **volatile oils** or **odoriferous gums/balsams**.
Perfumers use **Expression, Distillation, Maceration, and Absorption** to create products.
**Expression** extracts oil from citrus peels.
**Distillation** vaporizes and condenses essential oils.
**Maceration** soaks flowers in fat or oil to absorb fragrance.
**Absorption (Enfleurage)** is a cold process for delicate flower odors.
Simple perfumes are called **extracts**, while **bouquets** are complex mixtures.
The **1851 Exhibition** revealed new ottos.
**Allspice** oil is used in soaps.
**Almonds** provide highly esteemed, but **poisonous**, essential oil.
**Artificial otto of almonds (nitro-benzole)** is an alternative.
**Anise** oil is strong, suitable for soaps.
**Balm** is rarely used.
**Balsams** like Peru and Tolu provide agreeable smells and permanence to bouquets.
**Bergamot oil** is a useful, sweet-smelling perfume, sensitive to light, and used in **Ess. Bouquet**.

parts.title: Perfume Ingredients: Benzoin, Caraway, Cascarilla, and Cassia

sentences: **Benzoin**, a useful perfumer's substance, exudes from the Styrax benzoin tree and is mainly **imported from Borneo, Java, Sumatra, and Siam**.
The best type, from Siam, was called **Amygdaloides** due to its white, almond-like spots.
When heated, these spots produce a smoke that condenses into **flowers of benzoin** (benzoic acid), which retains the resin's odor.
**Extract or tincture of benzoin** serves as a good base for perfumes, providing **permanence and body**.
It's primarily used in making **pastilles** and **fictitious vanilla pomade**.
**Caraway oil**, distilled from Carum carui seeds, has a **pleasant, familiar smell** and is ideal for **perfuming soap**, especially in England.
When dissolved in spirit, it can combine with lavender and bergamot oils for **cheap essences**.
Ground caraway seeds are suitable for **sachet powder**.
**Cascarilla bark** is used in **pastilles** and for **perfuming rooms** (Eau à Bruler).

While the bark is mainly used for pastilles, the **Cascarilla gratissimus** leaves are fragrant and used as perfume by the Koras, suggesting perfumers should investigate distilling other fragrant Cascarilla species for **novelty**.
Messers.
Herring and Co. once distilled cascarilla oil, but it was only a curiosity.
**Cassia essential oil**, derived from Cinnamomum cassia bark, resembles cinnamon but is **inferior**.

parts.title: A Compendium of Perfume Ingredients and Extraction Methods

sentences: Lemon Grass otto is valued for soap and artificial verbena essence.
Lilac is frequently imitated due to high demand for scents similar to tuberose.
Lily fragrances are explored; natural lily scents are difficult to extract, but effective imitations exist.
Mace, Magnolia, and Marjoram have limited practical use for perfumers due to rarity or strong, specific odors, though artificial magnolias are popular.
Mignonette's natural fragrance is difficult to preserve in an essence, but a popular imitation is available.
**Flower farms in the British Isles** boost local perfumery and provide employment.
Mint ottos are used, especially for mouthwashes, and Myrtle has limited demand and is commonly imitated.
Neroli (Orange-Flower) produces two distinct odors from the same flower via different processes (maceration vs. distillation), used in various perfumes and soaps.
Nutmeg is rarely used in perfumery despite its fragrance, while Olibanum is used in incense, and Orange peel is used for essences like Lisbon Water and Eau de Portugal.
Dry bottles are important for these oil-based perfumes.
Orris (Iris) root possesses a pleasant violet-like scent and is used in sachets and as a fixative in bouquets.
Palm oil's fragrance extraction is unpromising.

parts.title: Perfumery Ingredients: Plant-Based Scents, Their Uses, and Market Overview

sentences: **Fragrant substances** in perfumery are diverse.
**Hungary water**, an early perfume, contained rosemary and was believed to offer **health benefits**.
**Santal-wood** is a prized scent, grown for **incense** and resistant to white ants.
**Otto of santal** is a dense extract for bouquets; **alcohol-dissolved ottos** prevent fabric stains.
Santal pairs well with rose.
**Fixatives** like storax and tolu extend the life of volatile perfumes.
**Tonquin (Tonka) beans** have a new hay scent from **coumarin** and are used in sachets.
**Tuberose** is an exquisite floral scent that requires **fixatives**.
**Vanilla** is used for extracts.
**Verbena** provides a lemon-like scent, frequently imitated.
**Violet** perfume is highly admired but rare, often imitated with blends.
**Vitivert** functions as a fixative.
There are import statistics for these substances, and **ambergris**, a mysterious whale substance, is used in perfumery.

parts.title: Ambergris, Civet, and Musk in Perfumery

sentences: **Ambergris**, once used as a perfume, was **incredibly overrated** despite its use.
An experiment even showed that a vessel used for human feces smelled like ambergris, leading to the speculation that its **perfume** is due to a similar **decomposition process**.
However, it is valued by perfumers for its ability to **make fleeting scents last longer** when mixed with other ingredients.
**Essence of Ambergris** is used for mixing, and when retailed, it is sweetened up and called **Extrait d'Ambre**.
This preparation includes rose, ambergris, musk, and vanilla extracts, creating a **lasting odor** that remains even after washing a handkerchief due to substances that cling to fabrics.
Powdered ambergris is also used in **cassolettes** (small perfumed boxes) and **peau d'Espagne** (Spanish skin) for perfuming paper and envelopes.
**Civet**, a secretion from the **civet cat**, was historically brought to Europe by the Dutch and is now sourced from Calicut and Bassora.
When confined, civet cats are kept in cages for **collecting the civet** twice a week.

In its pure form, civet has a **disgusting odor** to most, but when **highly diluted**, it becomes agreeable, a phenomenon common to many strong-smelling substances like certain **ottos** (essential oils).
For instance, otto of rose smells sickly alone but is delightful in small quantities.
Civet's odor is best imparted by placing it near **absorbent materials**, like spreading it on leather to perfume paper.

**Extract of Civet** is made by macerating civet and orris-root powder in rectified spirits and is mainly used as a **fixing ingredient** in delicate essences, with French perfumers using it more than English ones.
**Castor**, from beavers, is similar to civet but less commonly known in perfumery.

parts.title: Perfume Recipes and the Art of Fragrance Creation

sentences: The "Ess Bouquet" gained immense popularity, leading to many imitations, especially in Europe, trying to replicate the original from Bayley and Co.
The quality of spirit used is a critical factor; grape-derived spirit (French) and corn-derived spirit (English) each impart distinct aromas to the final product.
French spirit, with its œanthic ether, is ideal for citrine odors like Eau de Cologne, while British spirit is better for retaining the true aromas of substances like musk and violet.
While some ingredients are powerful and can mask others, delicate ones like violet require careful handling.
The adulteration of spirits with cheaper alternatives, like beet-root molasses or potato spirit, alters the characteristic odors of the final product.

The "Spring Flowers" perfume is particularly noted for its unique floral scent that is hard to imitate, mainly due to the specific preparation of rose and violet extracts, demonstrating the complexity and artistry involved in creating truly original fragrances.

parts.title: From Wet to Dry Perfumes: A Historical and Practical Overview

sentences: The **wet perfumery** branch, specifically **handkerchief perfumes**, concludes, with many recipes shared and many more existing.
The focus shifts to **dry perfumes**, including **sachet powders, tablets, pastilles, and fumigation** through heat and volatile resins.
Historically, ancient perfumes were primarily **odoriferous gums** from Eastern trees, valued highly as seen in religious texts.
Abstaining from perfume was a sign of **humiliation**.
Early Egyptian and Persian perfumes were all **dry**, using substances like spikenard, myrrh, and olibanum, many of which are still in use today.
An ancient Egyptian vase, 3000 years old, still emits a pleasant scent, suggesting its original use for **perfuming rooms**, similar to modern potpourri.

parts.title: The Art of Perfumed Soap: History, Types, and Remelting

sentences: The **ancient origins** of soapmaking date back to the **Gauls**, as reported by Pliny, and a soap-boiler's shop was found in **Pompeii**.
Early English soap trade records, dating to **1641**, highlight duties and patents.
Perfumers are not soap manufacturers; they are **"remelters"** who purchase raw soaps and modify them.
Soaps are broadly categorized into **hard (soda-based)** and **soft (potash-based)**, and they are further diversified by fatty matter and alkali proportions.
**Curd soap** is especially important to perfumers as the base for highly-scented varieties.
Various soap types include **Oil Soap**, **Castile Soap** (known for its marbled look), **Marine Soap**, and **Palm Soap**.
The **remelting process** involves cutting soap into thin slabs, melting them in a **steam-jacketed pan**, and **"crutching"** (stirring) to mix, color, and add perfume.
Soap is then poured into a **"frame"** to cool, cut into bars, and shaped into tablets or balls using presses and molds.
Special attention is given to **"variegated"** or **"marbled"** soaps, which are created by lightly mixing colors.

parts.title: Almond and Nut Pastes, Meals, and Emulsions

sentences: When making almond paste, it's crucial to **avoid burning** the almonds, as this creates an unpleasant smell.
The **vapor** released during the process is also **harmful**, so operators should stay away from it.
After the almonds are almost cooked, **add the remaining water**, then **rub the paste** thoroughly in a mortar.
Finally, incorporate the **perfume and spirit**.
Before packaging, the paste, along with honey paste, must be **sieved** to ensure a **uniform texture**, especially since almonds are difficult to grind smoothly.
Similar pastes like **Pâte de Pistache, Pâte de Cocos, and Pâte de Guimauve** are made similarly but should **not be confused** with confectioner's products.

The text also lists recipes for **Almond Meal** (ground almonds, wheat flour, orris-root powder, otto of lemon, almonds), and **Pistachio Nut Meal** (pistachio nuts, orris powder, otto of neroli, lemons), and mentions other perfumed meals like oatmeal and bran.
These preparations act as **soap substitutes** in lavatories, aiming to make the skin "**pliant, soft, and fair!**"

Recipes for **Emulsin au Jasmin** (saponaceous cream, simple syrup, almond oil, jasmine oil) and **Emulsin a le Violette** (saponaceous cream, syrup of violets, violet oil) are also provided, noting their **high cost** due to French oils, but acknowledging their **exquisite cosmetic qualities**.

parts.title: Hair Preparations: Pomatums, Dyes, and Depilatories

sentences: **Hair care products** include various **pomatums** and **oils**.
Recipes are provided for items such as **Balsam of Neroli**, **Marrow Cream**, and **Philicome**, with instructions for preparation, often by whisking until light and spongy.
The use of "**washed pomatums**" and "**washed oils**" is explained; these are residues from essence manufacturing that still possess enough fragrance for hair greases.
**Hair dyes** and **depilatories** have been used for personal adornment since ancient times.
Historical practices from Egypt, Moorish/Arab cultures, and Greece used natural substances like **kohhl** and **Henna** for coloring.

Modern recipes include **Turkish Hair Dye** (using galls and a metallic mixture), **Litharge Hair Dye**, and **Silver Dyes** (both simple and with mordants), with specific instructions for application and wear time.
Depilatories, or **rusmas**, are a means to remove unwanted hair, with a formula using **slaked lime** and **orpiment**, and require careful application due to their caustic nature.

parts.title: Perfumes, Hair Preparations, Glycerine, Essential Oils, and Flower Pigments

sentences: **Tincture of Myrrh with Eau de Cologne** can be prepared, and **Camphorated Eau de Cologne** can also be made.
Several **hair washes** are made, such as **Rosemary Water and Hair Wash**, **Athenian Water** and **Vegetable or Botanic Extract**.
**Bandolines**, which are hair-dressing preparations, are made utilizing gum tragacanth and different scents like rose and almond.
The **manufacture of glycerine** uses methods by Dr. Campbell Morfit and M. Jahn, with challenges regarding purity.
**Tests for alcohol in essential oils** employ acetate of potash and distillation.

The **coloring matters of flowers** are cyanine (blue/red) and xanthine/xantheine (yellow), and their properties and behavior under various chemical conditions are known, including the influence of plant juices and environmental factors on color.

parts.title: Artificial Fruit Essences and the Chemistry of Perfumery

sentences: **Artificial fruit essences** are created for various uses, particularly in **confectionery** and **perfumery**.
Methods exist for preparing compounds like **butyric ether** (pineapple oil), **acetate of amyloxide** (pear oil), and **valerianate of amyloxide** (apple oil) from basic chemical ingredients.
The process for pineapple oil involves **fermenting sugar** to produce butyric acid, which is then combined with alcohol and sulfuric acid to create the ether.
A debate exists about the **application of organic chemistry to perfumery**.

While some believe these artificial essences are revolutionizing perfumery, others, like Septimus Piesse, argue that these **fruit essences (ethers)** are primarily used for **flavoring food** (confectionery) and **not for traditional perfumes**, as they can have an intoxicating effect.
**Cow-house drainings** are not a main source of perfumes; instead, **natural flower cultivation** in places like France and Italy is important for perfume production.
Artificial compounds are useful for flavors, but they are distinct from the complex scents derived from natural flowers for fine perfumery.
